title: Life Strategies — Five-Minute Technique
metadata_mapping: Canonical frontmatter uses the existing entity schema. Richer recommendation metadata remains in this sidecar; the current search index does not automatically ingest these queries.

patterns.title: Five-Minute Technique
patterns.domain: Life patterns, everyday action, and wellbeing
patterns.short_description: Commit to five minutes of a task, then decide whether to continue using what the attempt reveals.
use_when: Starting feels like committing to a much longer session.
A concrete first action is feasible but motivation or confidence is being treated as a prerequisite.
A brief attempt can clarify the task or reveal a dependency.
goals: Make a credible, manageable starting commitment
Preserve an honest choice about continuing
mechanisms: Bound the initial duration rather than promising completion
Make contact with the actual task
Use the attempt to reassess interest, effort, and obstacles
Respect stopping as a valid outcome
patterns.estimated_practice_time: About eight minutes including a five-minute trial
not_ideal_when: The task is unsafe, infeasible, or requires substantially more setup than the trial permits.
The central problem is excessive workload, lack of resources, or an unresolved decision.
The short agreement is being used as a covert obligation to continue.
example_user_queries: I keep waiting to feel motivated before I begin.
Starting a task feels like giving up my whole afternoon.
How can I try something without promising to finish it?
I dread the report so much that I never open it.
What if I start and still do not want to continue?
I spend all my time preparing instead of doing the actual task.
I cannot tell whether I am avoiding the work or missing something I need.
I want a small way back into a hobby that feels demanding.
How do I make beginning feel manageable?
I keep turning a tiny commitment into a huge work session.
Can I stop after a short attempt without treating it as failure?
I want to find out whether motivation improves after I start.

practice.format: Optional offline guided practice with a user-started, non-blocking five-minute timer
practice.boundary: Records a plan, timer receipt, observations, and a chosen next move. Early continuation and cancellation remain available. It does not schedule work or infer that the user performed the activity.

visual.reason: Three contrasting examples show continuation, a discovered dependency, and stopping. A single flow could imply that continued work is the expected successful outcome.
visual.concept_graphic: A short accented starting segment reaches an ink decision point, with three equally weighted gray paths beyond it for continuing, stopping, or adjusting.

sources.title: NHS, Tackling your to-do list
sources.supports: An existing just-five-minutes strategy: start with a timer and reassess energy or willingness to continue.

sources.title: Centre for Clinical Interventions, Practical Strategies to Stop Procrastinating
sources.supports: Five-minute starts and other practical strategies, including task chunking; guidance rather than an isolated efficacy trial.

patterns.evidence_boundary: Existing self-help technique, not a claim of isolated efficacy or a uniquely effective duration. The proposed reasons it can help are practical explanations. Examples are fictional; improved motivation is optional.
